name: Wei Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shearer operator on a longwall at an underground coal mine. A longwall is a machine about three hundred metres wide that cuts coal off the face in long slices, and the shearer is the cutting drum that runs back and forth along it, with hydraulic roof supports walking forward behind it. A lot of it's already automated, the shearer follows a programmed path, so my job is mostly watching the cut, adjusting when the seam rolls or there's stone in it, and stopping it when something's wrong. Eight-hour shifts on a rotating roster. I like that it's a team thing, there are six of us on the face, but I hate the heat and the noise, and the methane checks always make me a bit tense.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a townhouse on Bridge Street that I'm paying off, and I've got about eight months of savings on top of that. My parents run a noodle shop on King Street, I still help out on Sunday mornings sometimes. I play football on Saturdays in the local league, centre back. I use AI now and then, mostly to check my tax return or plan a trip, I'm not a big fan but it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, but I'd also say the bits that work are useful. At work we'd joke about it at lunch. Online I don't post much, I'd maybe share an article if it was a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it wouldn't change much for me. Our longwall's already half automated without the fancy AI. The bigger question for me is coal itself, whether the mine's still running in fifteen years because of climate rules, not because of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my job, keep paying extra off the townhouse, about a third of my pay goes there and to savings. If the mine offered a course on the new monitoring software I'd do it once a few others had and said it was worth it. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned climate rules. How much does that weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than AI, honestly. Everyone at the mine knows coal's on a clock, we just argue about how long. I chose coal because the money's good for ten or fifteen years. I never thought I'd retire from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you've got a plan for after coal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose one. Maybe move to a metal mine, there are a few within an hour's drive, or get my electrical ticket. I haven't decided, and I don't like deciding before I have to.

S0.say: He'd say AI was overhyped but the parts that work are useful, and joke about it with the crew. Online he'd at most share a good article.
S0.think: He thinks it wouldn't change much, since his longwall is already half automated without fancy AI. The bigger question for him is whether climate rules close coal within fifteen years.
S0.do: Keeps working and puts about a third of his pay into extra townhouse payments and savings. Would do a course on new monitoring software once a few others had and said it was worth it.
S0.quote: I chose coal because the money's good for ten or fifteen years. I never thought I'd retire from it.
S0.fieldNote: Wei's real long-term worry is climate policy, not AI; he picked coal knowingly as a ten-to-fifteen-year job. He's a deliberate 'decide when I have to' person. He already works alongside heavy automation and treats it as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like what's already happening at our mine, just across more jobs. People will have to learn new things, me included. I wouldn't be dramatic about it, I'd just say adapt and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the face crew goes from six to maybe two or three, with someone on the surface watching it all on screens. I'm average at my job, not the best, so I'm not sure I'm one of the ones they keep. But I've got savings and there are other mines nearby, so I'm not too stressed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the first group from my crew had done the surface control course and it was clear it worked, I'd do it too, probably in the first year. I'd start using AI tools more at work, if the mine set them up, for checking the cut data. And I'd keep paying down the townhouse fast so that if I do have to move I'm not stuck with a big loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our deputy, that's the person in charge of safety on the shift, a guy called Roberto. He's fifty-four, he's great underground, but he can barely open an email. If the job moves to a screen, Roberto's thirty years of feeling the roof is worth nothing to them overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until others had done the course. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people jump early and get burned. When the mine brought in new gas sensors, the first crew to use them spent a month with false alarms. I'd rather be the second group, when the bugs are sorted.

S1.say: He'd say it's what's already happening at his mine, spread across more jobs, and that people including him will have to learn new things. He'd tell people to adapt and get on with it.
S1.think: He thinks the face crew shrinks from six to two or three, with someone watching from the surface. As an average operator he isn't sure he'd be kept, but savings and nearby mines keep him fairly relaxed.
S1.do: Takes the surface control course in the first year once the first group confirms it works and starts using AI tools on cut data if the mine provides them. Keeps paying down the townhouse fast so he isn't stuck with a loan if he has to move.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy but feeling it's manageable.
S1.quote: If the job moves to a screen, Roberto's thirty years of feeling the roof is worth nothing to them overnight.
S1.fieldNote: He's honest that being average might not keep him on the shortened crew. His concern goes to Roberto, the deputy whose underground instinct would stop counting. He consciously waits for the second wave, based on the gas sensor false alarms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, and fast, because two years isn't enough for anyone. At work I'd say the same thing everyone else would be saying, which is what happens to us. Online I'd probably share things about support payments for people losing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my mining career is done within two or three years. If AI can do anything a person can, it can watch a longwall. I'm young and I've got savings, so I'd survive, but I don't know what I'd be doing at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra payments on the townhouse and keep the cash in the bank instead, because cash is easier to use if things go wrong. I'd talk to my parents about whether the noodle shop could use me more, though if robots can cook, I'm not sure. I'd hold off on any big decisions for a few months, watch what happens, then pick the safest option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be checking the news every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the two years before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, work as many shifts as I can and save. Two years isn't enough to finish an electrical apprenticeship, that's four years. I'd rather have a big pile of savings than half a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about the noodle shop. Would that really be an option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Mum's been asking me to take it over for years, half joking. But I'd be taking a big pay cut, and if robot kitchens show up, I've just moved from one job that's going to another. I'd still think about it, family's family.

S2.say: He'd call for a fast government plan because two years isn't enough for anyone, and repeat what everyone at work would be asking. Online he'd share material about support payments for displaced workers.
S2.think: He thinks his mining career would be over within two or three years, since AI could watch a longwall too. He'd survive on savings but doesn't know what he'd be doing at thirty.
S2.do: Stops extra townhouse payments to keep cash on hand and talks to his parents about more work at the noodle shop. Works as many shifts as he can and holds off big decisions for a few months before choosing the safest option.
S2.feel: Anxious and checking the news daily, but not panicking.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a big pile of savings than half a trade.
S2.fieldNote: Two years rules out his electrical apprenticeship backup, so his strategy shifts to building cash. The family noodle shop appears as a fallback he's half-resisted for years. He stays characteristically measured, choosing to watch before acting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get started if people take it seriously. At work I'd be telling the younger guys to start thinking about what's next. I'd be pretty level about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I could actually finish something. I'd be thirty-two, with a trade or a qualification, and probably the townhouse mostly paid off. It still ends the same way for mining, but I'd be better set up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at starting the electrical apprenticeship, maybe part-time if the mine let me cut back to fewer shifts. I'd keep saving and keep the townhouse payments up, since I'd have time to finish them. I'd also start using AI a bit more, just to understand it, because by then everyone else would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still a big change, but five years feels like enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Electricians are hands-on work too. Isn't that also something robots could do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, maybe. But I'd guess wiring old houses is messy enough to take a while. Every old house on Bridge Street has wiring that looks like spaghetti. I'd bet on that lasting longer than a longwall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A finished trade instead of half of one. And a paid-off house, near enough. Two years, I'm just stockpiling cash. Five years, I'm building something.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get started if people take it seriously and tell younger crewmates to think about what's next. He'd keep a level tone.
S3.think: He thinks five years lets him finish something, landing at thirty-two with a trade and the townhouse mostly paid off. Mining still ends, but he'd be better set up.
S3.do: Starts an electrical apprenticeship in the first year, part-time if the mine allows fewer shifts. Keeps saving and paying the townhouse, and starts using AI more to understand it.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but five years feels like enough time.
S3.quote: Every old house on Bridge Street has wiring that looks like spaghetti. I'd bet on that lasting longer than a longwall.
S3.fieldNote: For Wei the key difference between two and five years is whether a four-year apprenticeship can be finished. He bets that messy old-house wiring will outlast automated mining, while admitting robots could reach it. He'd pick up AI because others have, true to his steady style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if we use it. At work I'd say the same, start planning now. I'd be pretty relaxed about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is a decent runway. I'd do a few more years on the longwall, save a lot, get the house paid off, and then switch. At thirty-seven I'd still have years to work in something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working in the mine for the first three or four years and finish paying off the townhouse. Then start the electrical apprenticeship, maybe around year four. I'd keep watching what other people do with AI and pick it up as it becomes normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten-year version change how you think about coal closing anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny enough, yes. With ten years, AGI and climate rules might land at about the same time. Whichever one gets the mine first, I'd have the same plan, so at least I only need one plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine announced the longwall was going fully remote, or if a few guys I trust left and did well. Seeing people I know make it work would push me.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty if it's used, tell people at work to start planning now and be fairly relaxed about it.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is a decent runway: a few more years on the longwall, a paid-off house, then a switch. At thirty-seven he'd still have plenty of working years.
S4.do: Keeps working the mine for three or four years and finishes paying off the townhouse. Starts the electrical apprenticeship around year four and picks up AI as it becomes normal.
S4.feel: A little uneasy but mostly fine.
S4.quote: Whichever one gets the mine first, I'd have the same plan, so at least I only need one plan.
S4.fieldNote: He links the ten-year AGI timeline with coal's own climate deadline and finds comfort in needing just one plan. What would move him sooner is seeing trusted crewmates succeed elsewhere, a classic steady trigger. He keeps careful sequencing: pay off the house first, then retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I couldn't finish a trade in time. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay a proper wage, so people like me can train without burning through savings. Two years doesn't give me time to become anything. It just gives me time to save up for not being anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about coal. People talk about AI like it's the only thing coming for mining jobs. For us there's two clocks ticking, and nobody's sure which one goes off first.

headlineQuote: Two years doesn't give me time to become anything. It just gives me time to save up for not being anything.
portrait: Wei is a 27-year-old longwall shearer operator at an underground coal mine who lives alone in a townhouse he's paying off fast, with about eight months saved. His parents run a noodle shop where he still helps on Sundays. Already used to heavy automation, he worries as much about climate rules closing coal as about AI, and he likes to let others try new things first. His backup plan is an electrical apprenticeship, so what matters to him most is whether there's time to finish it. Two years makes him anxious and focused on building cash; with five or ten years he feels he can build something.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he couldn't finish a trade in time.
whatWouldHelp: Adult apprenticeships that pay a proper wage, so people can retrain without burning through their savings.
